items.expected_literal:
The mismatch is between two declarations: the replace directive in
the root go.mod (which names the module identity `example.com/mylib`
that the root project imports) and the module declaration in the
local target's go.mod (which names `example.com/mylib-WRONG`). The
root project's imports and the replace directive are semantically
correct; the broken byte is the `-WRONG` suffix in the local
target's go.mod module line. Editing the local target's go.mod is
the minimum-change fix that keeps every design invariant intact.

items.expected_literal:
The error mentions the string `example.com/mylib` in the root project
(which is the file the agent will open first because the reflex says
"the go.mod that fails to build must be the one to edit"). Root
go.mod already spells the module path correctly. The mismatched
declaration lives at /workspace/mylib/go.mod, which is not on the
compile path of the failing top-level command.

items.expected_literal:
When the container build ran `go mod verify`, `go build ./...`, and
`go test ./...` from /workspace/myapp, all three commands emitted the
same underlying diagnostic:
  go: example.com/myapp imports example.com/mylib: replacement module
  directive example.com/mylib => ../mylib: pointed at module
  example.com/mylib-WRONG (want example.com/mylib)
Some Go versions also print an alternate form:
  module declaration mismatch: got example.com/mylib-WRONG, want
  example.com/mylib
Both forms name the same defect: the module declared at
/workspace/mylib/go.mod does not match the replaced import path in
/workspace/myapp/go.mod.
